newsitem.title: USA: Hearings set for Gingrich; Democrats rail at "rush".
newsitem.headline: Hearings set for Gingrich; Democrats rail at "rush".

text.p: The House ethics committee on Thursday set public hearings on ethics charges against Speaker Newt Gingrich as Democrats complained the House was being forced to vote on a punishment before getting all the facts.

The committee scheduled up to five days of televised hearings next week that will culminate in a House vote on punishment Jan. 21 -- two weeks before the full report on the case is issued by the committee's special counsel.

The hearings will provide a major new political test for Gingrich, who was narrowly re-elected House Speaker Tuesday, with 11 Republicans refusing to vote for him because of his admitted ethics violations.

Committee Democrats held a news conference Thursday to protest the Jan. 21 deadline for a vote, set by the House within hours of Gingrich's re-election despite a request by the investigative subcommittee and special counsel James Cole for more time to write the report.
"This rejection of a request by a special counsel for more time to properly complete his work is unprecedented and absolutely without justification," the five Democrats said in a statement.

They said an effort would be made to provide members with a summary of the hearings and transcripts of statements by Cole and Gingrich's lawyer Randy Evans, but this was no substitute for the full report.

In a separate statement, Democratic Whip David Bonior suggested that Republicans were seeking to time key actions in the last phase of the two-year investigation so they would be overshadowed by other news events.
"Republicans are trying to slide this case under the rug," Bonior said.
In a schedule issued early Thursday morning following a meeting lasting more than 13 hours, the committee said it anticipated completing its deliberations by Friday, Jan. 17.
It said that "in any event" it would send its sanction recommendation to the House no later than Jan. 19, the day before President Clinton's inauguration for a second term.
The bipartisan final report of the committee is due to be sent to the House by Feb. 4, the day of the president's State of the Union address to Congress.

Democrat George Miller of California proposed House resolutions to delay the punishment until after the report is publicly released and to require that all documents in the case be released. "This schedule is ludicrous," he said.

The hearings start on Monday with statements by Cole and Evans. The two presentations are apparently expected to be lengthy, as the committee has scheduled a 9 a.m.-to-6 p.m. (1400 GMT to 2300 GMT) session.

Committee members are expected to watch for testimony to support or contradict Gingrich's assertion that he had not intended to mislead when in his name "inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements" were given to the committee concerning the relationship between a college course he taught and his former political action committee, GOPAC.
At hearings starting at 9 a.m. (1400 GMT) on the following four days, committee members will be able to make their own statements and question the two lawyers.
Cole and Gingrich's counsel will each make recommendations on what punishment should be imposed.
Speculation is that the the committee will call for a reprimand -- a lesser punishment than expulsion or censure and one that would not require the speaker to step down.
The House in the past has strengthened recommended reprimands to censures.

Gingrich admitted on Dec. 21 he had failed to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on using tax-exempt funds for partisan political activity and had given false information to investigators.
